newsitem.title: GERMANY: German EMU debate prisoner of Bavarian politics.
newsitem.headline: German EMU debate prisoner of Bavarian politics.

text.p: Germany's EMU debate, a discussion Chancellor Helmut Kohl did not want to hold in public, has come out into the open in the most awkward way, entangled in the rough-and-tumble of Bavarian politics.

Germany's leading Eurosceptic, Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, has hoisted the political posturing and populism of his native state onto the national stage, forcing Kohl to stand up for super-strict convergence criteria for the euro.

The verbal ping-pong that followed has confused markets and managers, politicians and pundits. The Muencher Merkur daily ran a cartoon on Wednesday showing Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel standing behind a grumbling Stoiber.
"You're Bavarian," a confused Kohl says to Waigel. "Can you tell me what's going on in his head?"
In Frankfurt, analysts watching the debate have concluded it is almost completely political, the result of deep rivalries in Bavaria's ruling Christian Social Union (CSU) party.

"I try to understand it rationally, but I don't take it seriously anymore," remarked Adolf Rosenstock of the Industrial Bank of Japan. "The markets know 3.0 and 3.2 percent is no indicator of the strength or weakness of the euro."

The debate has bogged down over Stoiber's demand that Bonn meet the Maastricht deficit-to-GDP target of three percent exactly or delay Europe's monetary union. Kohl seems dead set on launching the euro in 1999, even with the larger deficits that economists say now seem inevitable.

Kohl's decision to embrace the 3.0 percent target, which critics say Stoiber has made into a fetish, seems more a tactical move to calm down the overheated debate than a real shift in economic policy, analysts agree.
So if Stoiber's political designs are behind all the fuss, what makes Edmund tick?

"He is haunted by the idea that he could lose the state election in 1998," said Alexander Gorkow, a journalist who covers Stoiber and Bavarian state politics for Munich's respected Sueddeutsche Zeitung.
"I don't know if he wants the euro or not. But everyone knows he wants to win the election at any price," he said.
Bavaria, a rich and deeply conservative state often called the "Texas of Germany," faces a state election in September 1998 that could end four decades of undisputed CSU rule.

Stoiber, 55, a hard-driving populist who was a key aide to Bavaria's legendary Franz Josef Strauss, took over as a "Mr Clean" premier in 1993 to clean up several local scandals and saved the CSU from possible defeat in 1994.
His 52.8 percent result, while better than expected, was still the worst showing for the CSU in decades and the long- term trend was for the party's support to crumble further.

Stoiber's chances worsened markedly in March of this year when the Free Voters Associations, a loose band of independent local politicians, announced they would put up candidates for the state assembly election for the first time.

The "Free Voters," mostly conservatives who have quit the CSU because of rivalries within the ruling party, won about 17 percent of the vote in local elections across Bavaria last year. They control one-third of all city halls in the state.

Political analysts estimate their support in a state poll at anywhere between five and 10 percent -- enough to deprive Stoiber of his absolute majority and possibly open the Munich- based assembly to a centre-left coalition.
"That would be like Chernobyl for the CSU," Gorkow commented. "If it loses the absolute majority, then anything is possible."

Another problem for Stoiber is that two issues which could cost him votes -- the launching of the euro and a possible increase in petrol taxes -- would be the work of his main rival, CSU chairman Waigel.
Stoiber, who would like to take over the party leadership, would be unable to stop either measure.

So Stoiber's option, political commentators agree, is to campaign against any national policy that unnerves worried rural Bavarian voters. Battling Bonn has always been popular with the Bavarians, whose defiant local patriotism has won them the label "Germany's Gaullists."
But the campaign itself does not seem suited to actually sabotage Kohl's dream of launching the euro.
"The euro will not fail because of Stoiber," the Hamburg weekly Die Zeit wrote. "It's not a war to the bitter end. Just a Bavarian show."
